title: Script Process
concept: After this one you can match a life story to the shape its plan takes over time, and say what that shape costs the person living it.
bookIdea: The script process is how a life script plays out over time, and it comes in six shapes: Until, After, Never, Always, Almost and Open-ended.

opener.setting: Wednesday, 8:40pm. Apartment 1A, Gran's sitting room, the television on mute. Her photo album is open on her knee, and Leo is on the floor beside her.

lines.text: “Look at this one. I was going to live properly once the children were settled. Everything was going to start then.”
lines.cue: turning an album page with one finger
eating a biscuit, not looking up

opener.ask: Every plan has a shape. Match each life story to the shape it takes over time, then say what the shape costs the person living it.

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Every life has a plan, and every plan has a shape. Three short stories. Pick the shape that fits each one.

items.text: “Once the bad year is over, we'll talk about the house. Not before.”
items.cue: a phone call, the television on mute behind him
items.why: The talk waits for a condition. Once the year is over, and not before, the conversation has a gate on it. That is 'not until': the plan says life starts when something else is done.

traps.1: This would be 'after this, the price' if he were having a treat now and paying for it later. Nothing pleasant is happening here. The house conversation is simply put off.
traps.2: This would be 'always the same' if the same talk kept coming back every Sunday. Here it is one postponed talk with a condition attached.

items.example: A parents' meeting at a school. The principal says the bus route will be discussed once the budget is approved, and the budget is still not approved in March.

items.who: A woman at a garden stall
items.text: “I've wanted a garden all my life. I read the seed catalogue every spring, and I never order anything.”
items.cue: turning the catalogue page, then closing it
items.why: She wants it, looks at it every spring, and never reaches for it. The wish and the not-getting go together. That is 'never gets it': the thing she wants stays on the page.

traps.1: This would be 'after this, the price' if she took a pleasure now and got a bill later. There is no treat here, only the wish.
traps.2: This would be 'plan runs out' if the plan simply had nothing written after a certain point. Her plan has a want in it, and the want never gets through the door.

items.example: A tenant who looks at the same flat listing every month and never rings the agent.

items.text: “Three runs short of the trophy in the final over. Second final in a row, and we fell at the last ball again.”
items.cue: holding up the scorecard, one finger on the number three
items.why: The plan got all the way to the last step and fell over it. That is 'almost makes it': close enough to count, and never through the door.

traps.1: This would be 'after this, the price' if they had a celebration now and a bill later. Nothing like that happened. The team simply lost the last over.
traps.2: This would be 'never gets it' if the team never reached the final. In this story they got there twice, and only the last ball got in the way.

items.example: A cookery competition. A baker reaches the final plate, then the oven timer rings too early and the cake sinks. She says “Next year” and means it.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Two boards of six. Each story is a plan with a shape. Match the story to the shape it takes over time, whatever the mood of the moment.

items.prompt: Six plans. Match each story to the shape it takes over time.

items.text: “I'll start living once the children are settled. Then I'll sit in the temple all morning, and nobody will need me.”
items.why: The living waits for a condition: the children settled. Until that happens, the plan has no start. That is 'not until'.

items.text: “One more round, then I'll be fine. The rent can wait. I'll pay for tonight next month, and the month after that too.”
items.why: The fun comes now and the bill comes later, and the bill keeps coming. That is 'after this, the price'.

items.text: “I've wanted a little place by the sea for thirty years. I read the listings every Sunday, and I never ring anyone.”
items.why: The want is real and old, and the person never reaches for it. That is 'never gets it'.

items.text: “Same call again. Mum asks about the money, I say the rent is fine, and we both go quiet until she asks again.”
items.why: Same question, same answer, same silence, every Sunday. The plan comes round again and again. That is 'always the same'.

items.text: “We had the deposit paid and the keys in sight, and then the owner backed out at the last signature. So close.”
items.why: The story stops one signature short of the finish. That is 'almost makes it': close enough to hurt, and never through the door.

items.text: “The children have all left home, and the house is quiet. I did everything I was meant to do, and I have no idea what the next bit is meant to be.”
items.why: The plan was clear up to a point and says nothing after it. The script has given out. That is 'plan runs out'.

items.prompt: Six more. Match each one to its shape.

items.text: “On-call again. It was me last time, and it'll be me on the next release too.”
items.why: The same scene, the same person, the same ending. The plan loops, and the loop is the shape. That is 'always the same'.

items.text: “I missed the final exam by one mark. Again. Third attempt, and one mark short each time.”
items.why: She keeps getting to the last step and falling short of it. The plan almost makes it every time. That is 'almost makes it'.

items.text: “I retire on Friday. There's a party and a cake, and then nothing planned at all. I never thought past the party.”
items.why: Everything is planned up to the party, and nothing after it. The script gives out at that point. That is 'plan runs out'.

items.text: “Once the holiday weekend rush is over, I'll talk to Daniel about the grade. Not before.”
items.why: The talk is parked behind one event, and nothing moves before it. That is 'not until': the start is tied to something else.

items.text: “Two weeks of late dinners and a weekend away feel great. The bill comes next month, with interest, and I'll sort it then.”
items.why: The late dinners are paid for later, and the cost grows before it lands. That is 'after this, the price'.

items.text: “I'd love to learn the cello. I look at them in the shop window most weeks. But that's not for people like me.”
items.why: The want is there, and the person talks themselves out of reaching for it. That is 'never gets it'.

items.text: “Gran's plan says live once the children are settled. Which explanation names the price of that plan?”
options: It is an Until script. Life waits for a condition, and the years of waiting are the price.
It is an Until script. Once the condition is met the plan ends well, so there is no price to pay.
It is an Always script. The same wait comes round each year, so the price is the same each year.
items.why: The books call this the Until script. The plan puts the start of living behind a condition, and the condition may take years to arrive. The price is the life not lived in the meantime, and it is paid every day.

traps.1: This reading would have everyone wish Gran well and move on. Nobody would ask what the waiting has cost her, and the years would simply vanish from the story.
traps.2: This reading would send the talk to the same argument every Sunday. The Until plan is a single postponed start, so the real price stays hidden.

items.example: A cousin who says “I'll start the course once the baby sleeps through the night.” Two years later the baby is a toddler, and the course is still on the list.

items.text: “A man retires on Friday. There is a party, a cake and a card, and nothing planned after it. Which shape is that, and what does it mean?”
items.cue: pen in hand, looking at the calendar
options: Open-ended: he is free to choose anything now, so the shape has no cost.
Open-ended: the script gives out at that point, and nothing is planned for what comes next.
Until: he is holding everything back until a condition is met.
items.why: The books call this the open-ended shape. The script runs out at a set point, and nothing is written for after it. Everything up to Friday was planned, and the party is where the plan stops. What it costs is a blank where the plan used to be.

traps.0: This reading would hear the gap as freedom. Nobody would ask what he will do on Monday, and the blank would arrive unprepared.
traps.2: Until would mean he was holding something back until a condition was met. Nothing is held back here. The plan has simply stopped.

items.example: A mother of grown-up children, Sunday. “I did all of it, and now the house is quiet and I don't know what comes next.”

debrief.nadia: Every plan has a shape, and most of them look harmless until you look at the price. Gran's wait has run for years, and a retirement party can end a plan overnight. Ask what the shape costs, and who pays the bill when the plan finally stops.
debrief.bookNote: The books call this the script process: how a life script plays out over time, in six shapes called Until, After, Never, Always, Almost and Open-ended.

reflection.prompt: Which shape did your own week look like most, and at what point in the week did you feel its price?
